transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Lowe (Head of Platform, Tidewater), Maya Ortiz (SRE), Evan Brooks (CTO)

Summary:
Tidewater is evaluating Redwood for inference serving for their customer-facing recommendation APIs. Primary concerns: graceful degradation under regional outages, multi-region routing, whether to run Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/onprem considerations), and SLA commitments for 99.9 vs 99.95. They want to validate fallbacks, KV cache behavior across regions, and auditability for compliance.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and traffic patterns
- Failure scenarios and acceptable degradation modes
- Fallback policy options (model variants, reduced context, degraded features)
- Multi-region routing and warm standby topology
- Security/compliance (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs)
- Benchmarking next steps and timeline

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining on a rainy wednesday, um we'll do quick intros, i'm alex, i'm the ae working with tidewater. priya is our solutions engineer, she'll run through the technical bits.
[00:20] Sam Lowe: Hey all, sam here, head of platform at tidewater. we mostly run our recommendation pipeline in GCP across us-east and eu-west.
[00:29] Evan Brooks: Evan, CTO. quick note — timeline is Q2 pilot, production in H2 if results look good.
[00:36] Maya Ortiz: Maya — SRE. i'll be digging into latency budgets and failover runbooks.
[00:42] Priya Nair: thanks. quick agenda: 1) understand failure modes, 2) map to redwood fallthrough options, 3) what infra fit (hosted/dedicated/private) looks like, 4) next steps for bench.

[01:05] Sam Lowe: to give context, our traffic peaks at 3M inference calls/day, 95th latency target is 120ms for the short prompt path. we have some heavy long-form re-ranks that are less latency sensitive. Cost is material — we need to optimize token cost without losing accuracy.

[01:38] Priya Nair: got it. when you say 120ms that's p95 or p50?
[01:42] Sam Lowe: p95, yes. p50 is ~40.

[01:45] Priya Nair: ok. two important levers for that are batching and KV prefix caching. redwood's runtime tries to keep KV cache warm and supports cross-request prefix caching, but in multi-region you have to choose whether caches are regional or replicated. that impacts cold-start behavior on failover.

[02:20] Maya Ortiz: can you clarify replication? we can't have cross-region synchronous replication for KV because of cost, so do you support warm failover where cache is rebuilt quickly?

[02:32] Priya Nair: yes — we support a warmed-standby approach. typical pattern: primary region serves live traffic with KV cache; standby region runs scaled-down replicas with pinned model variants so on failover we accept a temporary latency bump while KV warms. you can configure progressive roll-ups for cache priming, or use prefix-level cache snapshots. note — snapshotting is eventual, not transactional, so there will be divergence.

[03:10] Sam Lowe: sounds reasonable. how big of a latency hit do we usually see on switch? ballpark.

[03:16] Priya Nair: depends on workload and prompt reuse. for typical recommendation prompts we've seen p95 go from 120ms to 300–400ms for the first 10 minutes, then settle to 150–180ms. with pre-warmed standby and priming the common prefixes it's closer to 160–200ms.

[03:43] Evan Brooks: that first-10-min window is sensitive. our SLAs require us to maintain 99.9 availability and we need guidance on user-facing messaging during failover. can redwood support a partial degradation mode where we return cached short responses rather than fail?

[03:58] Alex Chen: absolutely. Redwood supports graceful degradation policies — you can define policy tiers: full model, lightweight distilled model, or cached responses. on host side you can configure automatic fallback to a smaller model or even a cached embedding lookup. we call it "degradation policy" in the console — sorry sometimes internal doc calls it fallback matrix.

[04:21] Maya Ortiz: question on model variants — if we fall back to a distilled model, how do we measure quality delta? we need regression alerts tied to a holdout set.

[04:30] Priya Nair: Redwood Optimize can run continuous quality checks against labeled prompt sets; you can set thresholds to trigger alerts and auto-rollbacks. those evals are parameterized per-route so you can compare top-k metrics across variants. small caveat, dataset labeling is on you but we integrate the eval harness.

[04:55] Sam Lowe: security: are audit logs and request-level metadata retained? we have compliance requirements around retention and KMS-managed keys.

[05:05] Alex Chen: yes — audit logs (request headers, route, model version) are available for Dedicated and Private with configurable retention. hosted plan also has logs but retention and PII controls are limited. we support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for Dedicated we integrate with cloud KMS as part of the contract.

[05:29] Maya Ortiz: do you have SOC2?

[05:31] Alex Chen: SOC 2 Type II, ISO is in progress. we'll share certs after the call.

[05:38] Evan Brooks: on network — we need VPC peering or private link for the pilot, can't go over public internet. how does hosted work there?

[05:47] Priya Nair: Hosted supports private networking via private link in select regions, but if you need full VPC control and egress restrictions, Dedicated or Private is the right path. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our tenancy but still managed control plane; Private is the fully customer-managed control plane you can run in your VPC or on-prem.

[06:15] Sam Lowe: budget question: what's the guidance on cost delta? we modeled both hosted and dedicated; we need a reality check on the break-even for tokens+gpu hours.

[06:25] Alex Chen: we'll send a cost sketch. as a rule of thumb, for steady high throughput workloads (3M calls/day with medium tokens) Dedicated often becomes cheaper at scale due to reserved capacity and better batching control. Hosted is faster to test with and lower friction to start. we'll include an appendix showing sample unit economics.

[06:52] Maya Ortiz: for the pilot we'll probably test hosted with private link to avoid ops lift, then evaluate Dedicated for H2. is that a typical path?

[06:59] Priya Nair: very common. pilot on Hosted with strict routing and SLA expectations, then lift to Dedicated once you validate latency and cost.

[07:10] Sam Lowe: question about SLA: hosted offers what nominally? 99.9? and Dedicated higher?

[07:18] Alex Chen: Hosted SLA is 99.9 in our standard public offering; Dedicated contracts can be 99.95 with SLO-backed credits depending on tier and commit. Private doesn't have our SLA since you manage control plane but we support runbooks and operational playbooks.

[07:36] Evan Brooks: for our legal team we'll need explicit outage impact matrices and credit calculations. can you share sample contract language?

[07:44] Alex Chen: yes i'll attach a redacted contract appendix.

[07:49] Maya Ortiz: digging into failure scenarios: what if an entire region goes down and we route to another region which has different quantization/kernel profile; do you do model variant mapping automatically?

[07:59] Priya Nair: yes — smart routing maps requests to compatible model artifacts; we maintain a catalog of compatible fallbacks. if a higher-precision model isn't available in the fallback region we can route to a quantized variant with a calibrated quality delta and you can set per-route acceptance thresholds. it's not magic — engineers define acceptable mappings and redwood enforces them.

[08:26] Sam Lowe: and what about circuit breakers / throttling?

[08:29] Priya Nair: the platform has per-route rate limits, queue depth controls, and circuit breakers that can return a synthetic response or 429 depending on policy. you can set traffic shaping so non-critical traffic is shed first.

[08:43] Evan Brooks: how do you test failover? we need a reproducible chaos runbook to simulate degraded caches, partial network partitions, and cold standby warmups.

[08:53] Priya Nair: we provide a chaos test harness and can run a joint tabletop exercise — typical steps: 1) simulate region outage in staging, 2) measure cold-start latencies, 3) exercise fallback mappings and ensure correct telemetry tags, 4) validate rollbacks. for Dedicated/Private we'll help run bench tests on your committed nodes.

[09:17] Sam Lowe: any gotchas around session affinity / conversational state when we failover? we have pinned sessions for some features.

[09:24] Priya Nair: yes session affinity is an operational concern. we recommend sticky routing by user-id to the same region for low-latency session state; when you failover we can transfer minimal session context using encrypted transfer, but full KV state is heavier. many customers accept transient context loss and reconsolidate. we'll map that in the runbook.

[09:45] Maya Ortiz: about data residency — some EU customers require that raw prompts never leave eu-west. hosted with private link — can we ensure that?

[09:54] Alex Chen: yes, region scoping allows you to pin routes to region-only model replicas. Hosted can enforce region-only policies for EU; Dedicated and Private give stronger contractual guarantees.

[10:03] Sam Lowe: ok good. timeline check: we'll need security review early next week, se deep-dive the following, then pilot sign-off.

[10:12] Priya Nair: suggested sequence: 1) send SOC2 and security docs (today/tomorrow), 2) schedule 90–120m benchmark deep-dive with maya and infra (week of Jan 12), 3) run a hosted pilot with private link for 2–4 weeks, capture metrics, then decide dedicated sizing.

[10:33] Evan Brooks: how do you instrument cost per request for our billing pipeline? we need token-level breakdown per route.

[10:39] Alex Chen: console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and model; you can export to your billing system or wire up webhooks. Dedicated gives more granularity and raw usage logs.

[10:52] Sam Lowe: any known limitations with our re-ranker flows that use long context windows? the 2-step ranker can hit 4–5k tokens occasionally.

[11:01] Priya Nair: supported but latency grows linearly with tokens. we recommend splitting or using KV caching for prefix-heavy contexts. we also have quantization profiles that help for longer sequences, but test is required.

[11:16] Maya Ortiz: one last question: if we accept degraded responses for 5% of traffic during an outage, how do we measure and surface that to downstream product teams?

[11:25] Priya Nair: you can tag responses with degradation metadata and set traffic sampling to send degraded responses to an evaluation pipeline. Optimize can also monitor quality metrics for degraded cohort and alert if drift exceeds thresholds.

[11:43] Alex Chen: quick recap and next steps — i'll send SOC2 and a redacted contract appendix, priya will assemble a bench runbook and suggested payloads, sam will share traffic percentiles and key prompts. let's schedule the se bench session for the week of Jan 12.

[11:58] Sam Lowe: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[12:02] Evan Brooks: thanks.

[12:05] Maya Ortiz: thanks all.
